title: Crimp a tube lug onto a 16 mm² cable in a bench crimping press, then lay the cable back on its rest
instruction: Crimp the cable lug sitting in the crimping press onto the cable's stripped end, then lay the cable, lug on, back on its rest and take both arms back to where they started.
context: Terminating stranded power cables with crimped compression lugs, which then bolt onto breakers, busbars, transformers and motor terminals, is regular work for electricians (about 821,000 US jobs in 2025 per BLS; O*NET tasks "Connect wires to circuit breakers, transformers, or other components" and "Install ground leads and connect power cables to equipment, such as motors") and for electrical and electronic equipment assemblers, control-panel builders among them (246,300 US jobs). The stripped end has to go fully into the lug's barrel and stay straight while the die closes, or the joint fails a pull test or overheats.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Distances are measured forward from the line between the arm bases and sideways from the midpoint between them. (1) A fixed steel pneumatic bench crimping press for cable lugs on the centre line, 30 cm forward, with a hexagonal 16 mm² die. In its die sits a tinned-copper tube cable lug for 16 mm² cable (a ring terminal with an M8 hole), whose barrel, 6 mm across inside and 16 mm long, points toward the arms, its axis 4.5 cm above the table, with a flared steel lead-in 2 cm across in front of its mouth. Its lever, which carries the upper die, is hinged 6.5 cm left of the barrel and reaches right; its red rubber grip is 14.5 cm right of the centre line. A spring holds the lever 12 degrees open (the grip 4.4 cm above closed); pushing it closed takes about 5 N on the grip, and closing it fully runs the press's air cylinder through one crimp. (2) A loose 16 mm² single-core PVC-insulated cable (H07V-R type, stiff), 16 cm long, 8 mm across and 30 g, its last 16 mm stripped to its stranded copper conductor, 5 mm across (the strip length matching the lug's barrel). It lies on two fixed black ABS-plastic V-rests along the forward direction, 12 cm left of the centre line, its bare tip 26.5 cm forward and 4.5 cm above the table. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Judged at the end of the trial. The crimp: the moment the lever first closes fully (within 1.5 degrees of closed), which closes the die on the barrel. A good crimp: then the bare end 13 to 16.5 mm into the 16 mm barrel (all but at most 3 mm of the copper in; the insulation, too wide to enter, stops on the lead-in within 3 mm of the barrel's mouth) and the cable within 8 degrees of the barrel's axis. Released: the lever back open at least 10 degrees and both grippers' fingertip centres (TCPs) at least 4 cm from its grip. Taken out: after the crimp, the cable's tip at least 4 cm from where the barrel's mouth was, the lug on it. On its rest: the cable's tip within 3 cm (across) and 1.5 cm (up or down) of where it lay, the cable within 20 degrees of lying along the rests. 1.0: a good crimp, released, taken out, laid back on its rest, and both arms back where they started (each fingertip centre within 5 cm of its start); 0.5: any crimp with the bare end in the barrel; 0.25: the bare end pushed at least 8 mm into the barrel at some point; else 0.0. In a real trial the depth is read after the crimp with a caliper as the bare gap between the insulation's end and the barrel's mouth (a 16 mm strip in a 16 mm barrel: a gap of at most 3 mm means at least 13 mm in), the cable's angle, its rest position and the arms from the overhead video, and a good crimp must also pass a pull test: the lug holds a steady 450 N pull on the cable (the UL 486A pull-out force for this size). The trial ends at the run limit, or once the full score has held for 1 s with the lever and the cable still.
reset_notes: Fit a fresh terminal in the crimper's die and lay a fresh stripped cable on its rests.
fidelity: Rigid-body simulation (Isaac Sim 6.1, PhysX, 20 Hz control). Simplified: the crimp is an event. When the lever closes, the task file reads where the cable's bare end is and, if it is in the barrel, swaps the lug for a crimped one that from then on goes where the cable goes (its hold is not tested in the simulation). The cable is a stiff rod; the press's air cylinder is not modelled: the lever is a hinge with a return spring. Cameras 1280 x 704 (Dream-1 sees 320 x 176).
